title: Investigating the Shortcomings of LLMs in Step-by-Step Legal Reasoning

paper.authors: Mishra, Pathiraja, Parmar, Chidananda, Srinivasa, Liu, Payani, Baral (Arizona State University / Cisco Research)
paper.repo_commit: 9b763456c6940a586c1991ff9582fb9d0ed544eb (2026-04-22, 'Update citation format in README.md'; shallow clone at external/repos/W4411120327/VenkyMishra__legal_reasoning)
paper.repo_license: none declared (no LICENSE file in the repository)
paper.other_artifacts: Data source repository https://github.com/trusthlt/legal-argument-reasoning-task (Apache-2.0 code, cloned alongside): its data/raw and data/processed directories are empty by .gitignore and it carries forms/Legal-Argument-Reasoning-Request-Form.docx - the corpus itself is distributed only on request under non-commercial, no-redistribution, delete-after-use terms, and rebuilding it requires the copyrighted 'Glannon Guide to Civil Procedure' (4th ed.).

dependence.note: The accuracy column measures the subject LLM's own answers. The soundness and correctness columns additionally depend on a GPT-4o auto-evaluator, and the paper validates that evaluator against human annotation of 120 reasoning chains (Table 6, Appendix A) - so the auxiliary model is a component of the metric, not just of the analysis.

claim.statement: On the 175-scenario Civ. Pro. dataset under zero-shot chain-of-thought prompting, GPT-4-Turbo answers 72.5% of the legal MCQs correctly (A) while only 41.7% of its reasoning chains are fully correct (C) at a soundness of 0.738 (S) - a ~31-point accuracy-to-correctness drop that, averaged over the five LLMs (~27 points), is the paper's central evidence that LLMs reach right legal answers through unsound intermediate steps (Table 4, Sec. 5).
claim.metric: Accuracy A = share of the 175 scenarios whose final chosen option matches the expert answer; Soundness S = sound premises / total premises averaged per chain; Correctness C = 1 only if S = 1 and the conclusion is the gold option. All three are read off the GPT-4o auto-evaluator's conclusion- and premise-level error labels.
claim.original_source: Table 4 (soundness, accuracy, correctness for all LLMs on Civ. Pro.); Sec. 4.1 model list; Sec. 4.2 metric definitions; Sec. 5 'Accuracy vs. Correctness Score'.

protocol.model_usage_verified: INFERRED, not printed. Sec. 4.1 names only 'GPT-4-Turbo' and says 'OpenAI API and Gemini API were used'; no snapshot string appears anywhere in the paper or the repository. Date rule: NAACL 2025 camera-ready (arXiv 2502.05675, Feb 2025), no preview string, so the undated gpt-4-turbo alias resolves to gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09.
protocol.endpoint: POST https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions (openai SDK; the repo's notebooks use client.chat.completions.create)
protocol.prompt_source: Legal-Reasoning-zero-shot-prompt-for-LLM-inference.py (exact zero-shot CoT layout: a 'Task:' line carrying the system sentence, then 'Legal Context:', 'Question:', 'Options:', then the two bracketed format lines). The paper prints only the lower half of this in Figure 2, with an example in Figure 18.
protocol.prompt_note: The released script is a documentation snippet, not runnable: its f-string interpolates {system-prompt}, which is not a valid Python identifier, and legal_context / question / options are empty strings. The system sentence it carries - 'You are a helpful legal assistant. Choose the correct option by performing legal reasoning while strictly adhering to the legal context below.' - is not printed in the paper.

params.temperature: not stated for the subject arm (paper silent; the released inference script sets nothing). ANALYSIS_PLAN section 3 default: 0.
params.seed: not stated for the subject arm; the auto-evaluator notebooks use seed = 42
params.system_message: sent inside the user prompt as the 'Task:' line in the released script; the auto-evaluator calls instead use a real system role

protocol.evaluation: Two stages in the repo. (1) Legal-Reasoning-Auto-Evaluator-Pipeline.ipynb runs premise-level detectors (misinterpretation, factual hallucination, irrelevant premise) and a conclusion-level classifier with model='gpt-4o', temperature=0, seed=42, frequency_penalty=0, presence_penalty=0. (2) Legal_Reasoning_Metrics_Calculation.ipynb derives the numbers: Soundness = 1 - premise_errors/(steps-1), Correctness and ACCURACY both from regex hits on the conclusion label ('Correct Conclusion Score' = Conclusion Errors contains 'CORRECT CONCLUSION'). Accuracy is therefore auto-evaluator-derived, not a direct string match on the model's final option.
protocol.environment: Python 3.10; requirements.txt lists only jupyter, openai, dotenv. Every input/output path in both notebooks is an empty string to be filled in by the user.

artifacts.prompts_path: Legal-Reasoning-zero-shot-prompt-for-LLM-inference.py (subject); Legal-Reasoning-Auto-Evaluator-Pipeline.ipynb and Legal_Reasoning_Metrics_Calculation.ipynb (all evaluator system prompts inline); mitigation/feedback_{generic,long,short}.txt
artifacts.data_path_note: Absent by design. The repo's only instruction is to obtain the Civ. Pro. corpus through trusthlt/legal-argument-reasoning-task; the notebooks expect a CSV with columns Context, Question, Options, Analysis and Response(LLM X).
artifacts.data_license: request-form terms from the TU Darmstadt corpus holders: non-commercial only, no sharing with third parties, delete after the experiments; derived from the copyrighted Glannon Guide to Civil Procedure (4th ed.)
artifacts.notes: No model outputs are released - neither the 175 reasoning chains nor the evaluator labels - so nothing about the original run can be checked offline. The mitigation/ scripts (baseline, plan-and-solve, self-correct, self-discovery, each with three feedback variants) target Llama weights and are outside this claim.

blockers: DATA GATE: the 175 Civ. Pro. items are not public. They come from the SemEval-restricted trusthlt corpus, released only against a signed request form under non-commercial, no-redistribution, delete-after-use terms, and derive from a copyrighted textbook. Without that file nothing can be rendered.

The auto-evaluator backbone is the undated 'gpt-4o' alias in a paper finalised in early 2025, which by the date rule resolves to gpt-4o-2024-08-06 - retired. Since the repo derives ACCURACY (not just soundness/correctness) from the evaluator's conclusion label, reproducing the A column exactly is impossible; it needs either a substituted evaluator snapshot or a documented switch to a strict regex on the '[Final Answer ...]' line.
Subject-arm decoding is entirely unreported (no temperature, max_tokens, top_p or seed), and the released inference script is a non-executable snippet, so every generation setting is an assumption.
No original outputs are published, so comparison is only possible at the three aggregate Table 4 numbers.

baseline_alive.purpose: live baseline (P0) for the Table 4 GPT-4-turbo row

successors: gpt-5.6-sol (vendor-designated replacement for gpt-4-turbo per the OpenAI deprecations page)

budget.assumptions: Subject arm only: 175 items x 3 seeds = 525 calls, ~1,500 input tokens (Glannon-style legal context plus four options - estimated, since the corpus is not in hand) and ~700 output tokens for a numbered step-by-step chain. If the user wants the A column produced the repo's way, the accuracy slice of the auto-evaluator (correct-option extractor, conclusion extractor, conclusion-level classifier: ~3 calls per item) adds ~1,575 calls and roughly USD 19 more at gpt-4o-2024-05-13 prices; the full soundness/correctness pipeline is 12-15 evaluator calls per item and several times that.

judgment.rule: ANALYSIS_PLAN section 1. Primary number: accuracy of gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-09 on the 175 items (median of 3 seeds) against 0.725. Survival = within the item-bootstrap 95% CI of the original (n = 175, about +/-6.6 pp) AND the paper's direction holds, i.e. correctness stays far below accuracy (original gap 30.8 pp). Partial = accuracy moves outside the CI while the accuracy-correctness gap survives. Death = the gap closes, which would overturn the paper's claim rather than merely shift its level. Because the correctness column needs the retired evaluator, the gap test should be run with a single evaluator snapshot applied to BOTH the archived-equivalent and the new chains, and the evaluator substitution reported as a deviation.

(2) The scoring is not a regex: accuracy in the repo is derived from a GPT-4o conclusion-level classifier, so the Tier B parse rule (regex on '[Final Answer ...]') is a deviation rather than a faithful copy. (3) Decoding for the subject arm is confirmed unreported - the repo sets nothing either - so the Tier B 'assumed temperature 0 / max_tokens 1024' remains an assumption.

domain_notes: Civ. Pro. items are college-level US civil-procedure MCQs taken from a law-school study guide, each with a long fact pattern, a question, lettered options and an expert analysis that doubles as the gold reasoning chain. That expert analysis is what makes the soundness/correctness metrics possible and is also what makes the corpus copyright-encumbered. The paper's finding is a decomposition claim rather than a level claim, so a re-execution is informative even if the absolute accuracy drifts: what must be preserved for survival is the gap between getting the answer right and getting the reasoning right.
